name: A course that breaks every rule once
summary: Enough of a small web server to rebuild its request checks and its weather cache yourself.

los.text: Build request checks that refuse unsafe POSTs
Build a cache for an outside service

capstone.spec: Rebuild a server with two routes, a host check and a JSON POST.

los.text: Explain how the server decides a request is safe

cta_summary.orientation: Three words you need before reading the server's checks.

tier_3_terminology_cards.concise_definition: The site a browser says a request came from.
tier_3_terminology_cards.project_anchor: The server compares it with its own address.
tier_3_terminology_cards.contrast_anchor: Unlike the Host header, it names the sender, not the receiver.
tier_3_terminology_cards.cloze_prompt: A browser sends the {{BLANK}} to say which site made the request.
tier_3_terminology_cards.try_first: How could a server tell which site sent a request?

tier_3_terminology_cards.concise_definition: The short list of names a server answers to.
tier_3_terminology_cards.project_anchor: Requests for any other name are refused.
tier_3_terminology_cards.contrast_anchor: Unlike a blocklist, anything not listed is refused.
tier_3_terminology_cards.cloze_prompt: The server only answers names on its {{BLANK}}.
tier_3_terminology_cards.try_first: Why might a server refuse a request for a name it doesn't know?

tier_3_terminology_cards.concise_definition: A rule that a change request must carry JSON, not a form.
tier_3_terminology_cards.project_anchor: A form from another site can't send JSON without asking first.
tier_3_terminology_cards.contrast_anchor: Unlike a form post, it needs the browser's permission across sites.
tier_3_terminology_cards.cloze_prompt: Requiring a {{BLANK}} stops plain forms on other sites from changing anything.
tier_3_terminology_cards.try_first: What kind of request can any web page send without asking?

lessons.name: Why a cross-site POST is refused

los.text: Understand why the server refuses a POST from another site

source_ref.cite: Barth, A., Jackson, C. and Mitchell, J. C. (2008). Robust defenses for cross-site request forgery. ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security.

metadata.module_name: Why a cross-site POST is refused

cta_summary.orientation: Any page you visit can try to send a request to your server. This lesson is why that fails.

tier_2_self_explanation_cards.front_prompt: Why does the server refuse a POST whose Origin is another site?
tier_2_self_explanation_cards.back_explanation: Any page can make your browser send a request, with your access. Checking the Origin means only the server's own page can change things.

eval_rubric.idea: another page can send requests as you
only the server's own page may change things

key_ideas: A browser sends requests for any page you visit.
The Origin header names the page that asked.
preread.try_first: If any page can make your browser send a request, what stops a stranger's page?

tier_2_self_explanation_cards.front_prompt: The check is changed to accept a POST when the Origin header is missing. What can go wrong?
tier_2_self_explanation_cards.back_explanation: Some requests arrive without an Origin. If a missing one is let through, a stranger's page can still change things.

eval_rubric.idea: a request can arrive without the header

key_ideas: Not every request carries an Origin header.
preread.try_first: What should a check do when the thing it checks is missing?

tier_2_self_explanation_cards.front_prompt: In two sentences: what attack does the Origin check stop, and how?
tier_2_self_explanation_cards.back_explanation: It stops a page on another site from using your browser to change things. The server only accepts changes whose Origin is its own page.

eval_rubric.idea: only its own origin is accepted

key_ideas: The check compares the Origin with the server's own.
preread.try_first: Who sends the request in this attack: you, or a page you happened to open?

los.text: Explain how the weather cache saves calls to the outside service
Choose when the server should fetch the weather again

cta_summary.orientation: The weather changes slowly, so asking for it on every page view wastes calls.

tier_2_self_explanation_cards.front_prompt: Fetch the weather on every page view, or keep it for ten minutes? Choose and say why.
tier_2_self_explanation_cards.back_explanation: Keep it for ten minutes: the weather barely changes in that time, and the outside service limits how often you may ask.

key_ideas: Outside services limit how often you may ask.
Weather changes over hours, not seconds.
preread.try_first: How often does the weather outside really change?

tier_2_self_explanation_cards.front_prompt: The outside service is down. Show the last reading, or show nothing? Choose and say why.
tier_2_self_explanation_cards.back_explanation: Show the last reading, marked as old: a slightly old answer is more useful than none, as long as it says so.

key_ideas: A reading can be shown with its age.
preread.try_first: Would you rather see yesterday's forecast, or a blank?

tier_2_self_explanation_cards.front_prompt: A page asks for the weather twice in one minute. What should the server do the second time, and why?
tier_2_self_explanation_cards.back_explanation: Answer from the saved reading: it is fresh enough, and asking again would spend a call for nothing.

key_ideas: A saved reading has an age.
preread.try_first: What does the server already have after the first request?
